title: Prehistory: from the first humans to the first farms
length_note: Ten classes. The story has ten parts that each need the one before: how we know, early ancestors, tools, fire, first migrations, our own species, art and symbols, the Ice Age, first farms, and first villages. Fewer classes would squash the debates, which you asked to keep. More would repeat material. Most classes run 25 minutes. The densest ones run 30, and the lightest runs 20. Each class has one main idea and can be done in a single sitting, with a short recap at the start. That suits people relearning after a brain injury as well as teenagers. Every class marks where scientists disagree and gives both sides. Dates and species names change as new finds come in, so every class is flagged for research with sources before it is written.

classes.title: How we know: reading the deep past without writing
classes.goal: Explain what 'prehistory' means, name the main kinds of evidence (bones, tools, DNA, dating methods), and say why dates and stories are sometimes revised.
topics: What prehistory means and why there are no written records
Fossils, tools, hearths, and ancient DNA
Basic dating ideas: radiocarbon and other methods, and why each has a limit
Why evidence is patchy, and how new finds change the story
Timeline overview of the whole course

classes.title: Walking upright: the first human relatives
classes.goal: Describe what hominins are, why walking on two legs matters, and name two or three early hominins and what we know about them.
topics: Our place among the apes
Early hominins and Australopithecus
Bipedalism: the evidence and the competing explanations for why it began
Disagreement: how to arrange the family tree, and which species are direct ancestors versus cousins

classes.title: The first stone tools
classes.goal: Tell apart the main early stone-tool traditions, say what they were used for, and explain the debate over who made the very first tools.
topics: What counts as a tool, and how archaeologists tell a made tool from a broken rock
Oldowan chopping and flaking tools
Acheulean hand axes and what they suggest about planning
Cut-marked bones and early meat-eating
Disagreement: which species made the earliest tools, and how early tool use began

classes.title: Fire and the changing body
classes.goal: Explain how fire changed daily life, and describe the debate over when people first controlled it.
topics: Using fire versus making and keeping fire
What the early evidence for hearths looks like, and why it is hard to read
Warmth, protection, light, and cooked food
Disagreement: when regular fire use began, and how much cooking drove bigger brains
Homo erectus and changes in body and brain

classes.title: Leaving Africa the first time
classes.goal: Describe the early spread of Homo beyond Africa, and name the main sites and species involved.
topics: Why Africa is the starting point
Early dispersals of Homo erectus and related groups into Asia and Europe
Key sites and what they show
Other human species, such as the 'hobbit' of Flores and Homo naledi, and what is still debated
Disagreement: how many dispersals there were, and how species should be named and divided

classes.title: Our species, our cousins: Homo sapiens, Neanderthals and Denisovans
classes.goal: Explain where Homo sapiens came from, what ancient DNA shows about mixing with other humans, and how the two main models of origin differ.
topics: Neanderthals: life, tools, and range
Denisovans and what DNA reveals
Where and when Homo sapiens appeared
Disagreement: a single African origin versus a wider 'pan-African' or multiregional picture
Interbreeding and the DNA many people carry today
Disagreement: why Neanderthals disappeared

classes.title: Spreading across the world
classes.goal: Trace the main routes by which Homo sapiens reached Asia, Australia, Europe and the Americas, and explain why the dates are argued over.
topics: Routes and timing of the main migrations
Crossing water to Australia
Europe and the arrival of Homo sapiens
Peopling of the Americas: the coastal route, the ice-free corridor, and newer finds
Disagreement: how early people reached the Americas, with old and new evidence

classes.title: Art, symbols and the mind: cave paintings and beyond
classes.goal: Describe the main forms of early symbolic behaviour and weigh the debate on when and by whom it began.
topics: Cave art in Europe, Indonesia and elsewhere
Ornaments, pigments, carved figures, and music
Dating art and the problems with it
Disagreement: did Neanderthals make art, and did symbolic thinking appear suddenly or slowly?
Possible meanings of the art, and why we cannot be sure

classes.title: The Ice Age world
classes.goal: Explain how Ice Age climate shaped where and how people lived, and describe the two main explanations for the loss of large animals.
topics: Glacial and warmer periods, and the coldest stretch of the last Ice Age
Hunter-gatherer life: food, shelter, clothing, and travel
Tools and technology of the period
Large Ice Age animals
Disagreement: were big animals lost mainly to climate change, to human hunting, or to both?

classes.title: The first farms and villages
classes.goal: Describe where and how farming began, why scientists disagree about the causes, and what changed when people settled in villages.
topics: The end of the Ice Age and a warmer, wetter world
Early settled people before farming
The Fertile Crescent and the first crops and animals
Independent starts to farming in other regions
Disagreement: why farming began (climate, population pressure, feasting and ritual, gradual experiment)
Early villages and towns: houses, food storage, health, and inequality
Disagreement: did farming spread by moving people or by spreading ideas?
Where prehistory ends and written history begins
